\(0.555\) is a terminating decimal with 3 digits after the point, so write it over \(1000\).
So \(0.555=\frac{555}{1000}\).

Let \(x=29.\overline{568}=29.568568\ldots\). The block has 3 digits, so multiply by \(1000\):
\(1000x=29568.568568\ldots\)
Subtracting, \(1000x-x=29568.568\ldots-29.568\ldots\), so \(999x=29539\).
So \(29.\overline{568}=\frac{29539}{999}\).

Here \(9.315\,315\ldots=9.\overline{315}\). Let \(x=9.\overline{315}\); the block has 3 digits, so multiply by \(1000\):
\(1000x=9315.315315\ldots\)
Subtracting, \(999x=9315-9=9306\).
So \(9.315\,315\ldots=\frac{9306}{999}\).

Let \(x=30.\overline{219}=30.219219\ldots\). The block has 3 digits, so multiply by \(1000\):
\(1000x=30219.219219\ldots\)
Subtracting, \(999x=30219-30=30189\).
So \(30.\overline{219}=\frac{30189}{999}\).

Divide \(5\) by \(7\): the remainders repeat after six steps, giving the digits \(714285\) over and over.
So \(\frac{-5}{7}=-0.\overline{714285}\).

Divide \(9\) by \(11\): the remainders \(9\) and \(2\) repeat, giving the digits \(81\) over and over.
So \(\frac{9}{11}=0.\overline{81}\).

\(5\) is not a perfect square, so \(\sqrt{5}\) is irrational and its decimal form is non-terminating and non-recurring.
So \(\sqrt{5}=2.2360679\ldots\)

Divide \(121\) by \(13\): the quotient starts at \(9\) with remainder \(4\), and thereafter the block of digits \(307692\) repeats.
So \(\frac{121}{13}=9.\overline{307692}\).

The denominator is \(8=2^{3}\), so the division terminates: \(29\div 8=3\) with remainder \(5\), and \(\frac{5}{8}=0.625\).
So \(\frac{29}{8}=3.625\).

Suppose, if possible, that \(5+\sqrt{7}\) is rational. Then \(5+\sqrt{7}=\frac{p}{q}\) for some integers \(p,q\) with \(q\ne 0\).
So \(\sqrt{7}=\frac{p}{q}-5=\frac{p-5q}{q}\), and the right side is a quotient of two integers with non-zero denominator, i.e. a rational number.
That makes \(\sqrt{7}\) rational. But \(7\) is not a perfect square, so \(\sqrt{7}\) is irrational — a contradiction.
Hence our supposition is wrong, and \(5+\sqrt{7}\) is an irrational number.

\(\sqrt{8}=\sqrt{4\times 2}=2\sqrt{2}\).
So \(\frac{3}{4}\sqrt{8}=\frac{3}{4}\times 2\sqrt{2}=\frac{3}{2}\sqrt{2}\).

\(\sqrt{45}=\sqrt{9\times 5}=3\sqrt{5}\).
So \(-\frac{5}{9}\sqrt{45}=-\frac{5}{9}\times 3\sqrt{5}=-\frac{5}{3}\sqrt{5}\).

\(\sqrt{32}=\sqrt{16\times 2}=4\sqrt{2}\). Multiplying by \(\sqrt{2}\) gives \(4\sqrt{2}\times\sqrt{2}=8\), a rational number.
So the simplest rationalising factor is \(\sqrt{2}\).

\(\sqrt{50}=\sqrt{25\times 2}=5\sqrt{2}\). Multiplying by \(\sqrt{2}\) gives \(5\sqrt{2}\times\sqrt{2}=10\), a rational number.
So the simplest rationalising factor is \(\sqrt{2}\).

\(\sqrt{27}=\sqrt{9\times 3}=3\sqrt{3}\). Multiplying by \(\sqrt{3}\) gives \(3\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{3}=9\), a rational number.
So the simplest rationalising factor is \(\sqrt{3}\).

\(\sqrt{10}\) has no square factor to take out. Multiplying by \(\sqrt{10}\) gives \(\frac{3}{5}\sqrt{10}\times\sqrt{10}=\frac{3}{5}\times 10=6\), a rational number.
So the simplest rationalising factor is \(\sqrt{10}\).

\(3\sqrt{72}=3\sqrt{36\times 2}=3\times 6\sqrt{2}=18\sqrt{2}\). Multiplying by \(\sqrt{2}\) gives \(18\sqrt{2}\times\sqrt{2}=36\), a rational number.
So the simplest rationalising factor is \(\sqrt{2}\).

\(11\) has no square factor, so \(4\sqrt{11}\) is already in simplest form. Multiplying by \(\sqrt{11}\) gives \(4\sqrt{11}\times\sqrt{11}=44\), a rational number.
So the simplest rationalising factor is \(\sqrt{11}\).

Write each surd in simplest form: \(\sqrt{147}=7\sqrt{3}\), \(\sqrt{192}=8\sqrt{3}\), \(\sqrt{75}=5\sqrt{3}\).
So the expression \(=\frac{4}{7}\times 7\sqrt{3}+\frac{3}{8}\times 8\sqrt{3}-\frac{1}{5}\times 5\sqrt{3}=4\sqrt{3}+3\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{3}\).
These are like surds, so the answer is \(6\sqrt{3}\).

\(2\sqrt{27}=2\times 3\sqrt{3}=6\sqrt{3}\), and rationalising, \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}=\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{3}\).
So the expression \(=5\sqrt{3}+6\sqrt{3}+\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{3}=\left(5+6+\frac{1}{3}\right)\sqrt{3}\).
So the answer is \(\frac{34}{3}\sqrt{3}\).

\(\sqrt{216}=\sqrt{36\times 6}=6\sqrt{6}\), \(\sqrt{294}=\sqrt{49\times 6}=7\sqrt{6}\), and \(\frac{3}{\sqrt{6}}=\frac{3\sqrt{6}}{6}=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{6}\).
So the expression \(=6\sqrt{6}-5\sqrt{6}+7\sqrt{6}-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{6}=\left(6-5+7-\frac{1}{2}\right)\sqrt{6}\).
So the answer is \(\frac{15}{2}\sqrt{6}\).

\(4\sqrt{12}=4\times 2\sqrt{3}=8\sqrt{3}\), \(\sqrt{75}=5\sqrt{3}\), \(7\sqrt{48}=7\times 4\sqrt{3}=28\sqrt{3}\).
So the expression \(=8\sqrt{3}-5\sqrt{3}-28\sqrt{3}=(8-5-28)\sqrt{3}\).
So the answer is \(-25\sqrt{3}\).

\(2\sqrt{48}=2\times 4\sqrt{3}=8\sqrt{3}\), \(\sqrt{75}=5\sqrt{3}\), and rationalising, \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}=\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{3}\).
So the expression \(=8\sqrt{3}-5\sqrt{3}-\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{3}=\left(8-5-\frac{1}{3}\right)\sqrt{3}\).
So the answer is \(\frac{8}{3}\sqrt{3}\).

Multiply numerator and denominator by \(\sqrt{5}\):
\(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}=\frac{1\times\sqrt{5}}{\sqrt{5}\times\sqrt{5}}=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\).
So the answer is \(\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\).

Multiply numerator and denominator by \(\sqrt{7}\):
\(\frac{2}{3\sqrt{7}}=\frac{2\times\sqrt{7}}{3\sqrt{7}\times\sqrt{7}}=\frac{2\sqrt{7}}{3\times 7}\).
So the answer is \(\frac{2\sqrt{7}}{21}\).

The conjugate of \(\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{2}\) is \(\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{2}\). Multiply numerator and denominator by it:
\(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{2}}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}-(\sqrt{2})^{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{2}}{3-2}\).
So the answer is \(\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{2}\).

Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate \(3\sqrt{5}-2\sqrt{2}\):
denominator \(=(3\sqrt{5})^{2}-(2\sqrt{2})^{2}=45-8=37\).
So \(\frac{1}{3\sqrt{5}+2\sqrt{2}}=\frac{3\sqrt{5}-2\sqrt{2}}{37}\).

Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate \(4\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{2}\):
denominator \(=(4\sqrt{3})^{2}-(\sqrt{2})^{2}=48-2=46\).
So \(\frac{12}{4\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{2}}=\frac{12(4\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{2})}{46}=\frac{6(4\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{2})}{23}\).
